title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
The Four Atomic Vector Types
In R, every element in an atomic vector must have the same type:


1. Numeric (Double)
Decimal numbers (default in R):
weights <- c(68.5, 72.0, 81.3)
typeof(weights) # "double"
2. Integer
Explicit whole numbers with L:
counts <- c(1L, 5L, 12L)
typeof(counts)  # "integer"

3. Character (Strings)
Text enclosed in quotes:
drugs <- c("aspirin", "statin", "placebo")
typeof(drugs)   # "character"
4. Logical (Booleans)
TRUE or FALSE (all caps):
adherent <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
typeof(adherent)# "logical"

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
The Type Hierarchy & Implicit Coercion
What happens when you mix different types in c(...)?
R silently converts everything to the least restrictive type:
\[\text{logical} \longrightarrow \text{integer} \longrightarrow \text{double} \longrightarrow \text{character}\]
# Logical to numeric (TRUE becomes 1, FALSE becomes 0)
sum(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE))  # Count how many TRUEs: 3
mean(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE))# Proportion of TRUEs: 0.5

# Numeric + Character becomes Character
c(10, 25, "missing")             # c("10", "25", "missing")






Pro-Tip for Health Data


mean(bp > 140, na.rm = TRUE) directly calculates the prevalence of hypertension by coercing logicals to 1s and 0s!

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Summary Statistics on Vectors
R has built-in vector aggregators:
chol <- c(185, 220, 240, 195, 210, NA)

length(chol)              # Total elements including NA (6)
sum(is.na(chol))          # Count missing values (1)
mean(chol, na.rm = TRUE)  # Arithmetic mean (212)
sd(chol, na.rm = TRUE)    # Standard deviation (20.8)
summary(chol)             # 5-number summary + Mean + NAs

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Repetition with rep()
The rep() function replicates values using times or each:


times (Pattern repetition)
Repeats the whole vector:
rep(c("A", "B"), times = 3)
# "A" "B" "A" "B" "A" "B"

# Unequal repetitions per element:
rep(c("Control", "Treated"), times = c(4, 2))
# "Control" "Control" "Control" "Control" "Treated" "Treated"

each (Element repetition)
Repeats each item before moving to next:
rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3)
# "A" "A" "A" "B" "B" "B"

# Combining both:
rep(c("Dose1", "Dose2"), each = 2, times = 2)
# "Dose1" "Dose1" "Dose2" "Dose2" "Dose1" "Dose1" "Dose2" "Dose2"

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Modulo Arithmetic %%
The modulo operator %% calculates the remainder of division:
14 %% 3   # 2  (14 = 4 * 3 + 2)
10 %% 2   # 0  (10 is even)






Common Applications in Data Science



Even numbers: x %% 2 == 0
Divisible by 5: x %% 5 == 0
Assigning participants to \(K\) rotating study groups: (1:N) %% K + 1

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
The Three Subsetting Methods
We extract elements using square brackets x[...]:
ages <- c(23, 45, 19, 31, 56, 42)


1. Positive Indices
Extract by position (1-indexed):
ages[1]        # 23
ages[c(1, 4)]  # 23 31
ages[2:4]      # 45 19 31

2. Negative Indices
Exclude specific positions:
ages[-1]       # All except 1st
ages[-c(2, 5)] # Drop 2nd & 5th
# ages[-2:4]   # ERROR! Use -(2:4)

3. Logical Subsetting
Extract where TRUE:
ages[ages > 40]
# 45 56 42

ages[ages >= 30 & ages <= 50]
# 45 31 42

Logical Operators for Filtering
Combine conditions using element-wise logical operators:








Operator
Meaning
Example




&
Element-wise AND (both true)
(bmi > 25) & (age > 50)


\|
Element-wise OR (either true)
(status == "Severe") \| (fever == TRUE)


!
Logical NOT (inversion)
!(city %in% c("NY", "CA"))


%in%
Value matching (set membership)
id %in% confirmed_cases

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Modifying Vectors in Place (Mutation)
Use subsetting on the left side of <- to update specific elements:
scores <- c(88, -99, 95, -99, 72)

# Replace survey code -99 with NA:
scores[scores == -99] <- NA
scores
# 88 NA 95 NA 72

# Cap values at 90 (winsorizing):
scores[scores > 90 & !is.na(scores)] <- 90
scores
# 88 NA 90 NA 72

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Sorting, Ranking, and Ordering
Understanding the difference between sort(), rank(), and order():
vals <- c(30, 10, 50, 20)


sort(x)
Returns sorted values:
sort(vals)
# 10 20 30 50

sort(vals, decreasing = TRUE)
# 50 30 20 10

rank(x)
Returns rank position of each element:
rank(vals)
# 3 1 4 2
# (30 is 3rd, 10 is 1st, etc.)

order(x)
Returns indices that would sort x:
order(vals)
# 2 4 1 3
vals[order(vals)] # sorted!

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Handling Ties in rank()
When numbers repeat, how should ranks be assigned?
scores <- c(80, 95, 80, 70)

rank(scores)                        # Default: average ranks (2.5 4.0 2.5 1.0)
rank(scores, ties.method = "first") # By appearance: (2 4 3 1)
rank(scores, ties.method = "min")   # Sports ranking: (2 4 2 1)






Tip


ties.method = "first" is essential for deterministic top-\(K\) rankings in data pipelines!

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
AI Corner: Beware Vector Recycling!
When R operates on vectors of different lengths, it silently recycles the shorter one:


What R Does:
x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
y <- c(1, 2)
x + y
# Computes: 10+1, 20+2, 30+1, 40+2
# Output: 11 22 31 42

⚠️ The Danger with AI:

LLMs often generate code that accidentally recycles vectors when filtering or standardizing.
Always check length(x) == length(y) before element-wise operations!

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text: This course treats AI coding assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and similar) as professional tools: you will learn to use them effectively and critically, and you will also develop the individual fluency to program without them.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text:
Why this policy
Statistical programmers now work alongside AI tools daily. Banning them would prepare you for a world that no longer exists; letting them do your thinking would leave you unable to catch their mistakes, and they make plenty. The course therefore teaches the skill that actually matters: directing AI tools and verifying their output. Week 8 is a dedicated workshop, and every week includes a short “AI corner” showing one good and one bad AI use for that week’s topic.
Free-tier AI tools are sufficient for all coursework; no paid subscriptions are required or expected.
Submitting AI-generated work you do not understand, using AI during a quiz, or omitting required disclosure is an academic-integrity violation.

title: RStudio projects and cloning a repository
text:
An RStudio project is a folder with an .Rproj file in it. That one file changes how RStudio behaves in three ways that save you hours:

The working directory is the project folder. Every file path in your code can be written relative to the project, so read_csv("data/survey.csv") works on your laptop, on a lab machine, and on your grader’s computer. You never need setwd() again, and you should never use it.
Each project gets its own session. Open two projects and you get two separate R sessions, with their own environments and command histories. Work on one analysis does not leak into another.
RStudio shows you the Git tab. Version control only appears when the folder RStudio has open is a Git repository and an RStudio project.

The rule that follows from this: always open your work by opening the project, never by opening a single .R or .qmd file from your file browser. Opening a loose file gives you the editor without the working directory, without the Git tab, and with paths that break.

title: RStudio projects and cloning a repository
section: Keep your projects in one folder
text:
Keep your projects in one folder
Before you clone anything, decide where projects live and stick to it. One folder in your home directory, holding one subfolder per project:
~/gph2182/
  weekly-exercise-01-yourusername/
  weekly-exercise-02-yourusername/
  in-class-exercises-yourusername/
This matters more than it sounds. Over a semester you accumulate a dozen repositories, and if they are scattered across Desktop, Downloads, and a half-synced cloud folder, you will lose one. With a single parent folder, switching between them is File > Recent Projects.






WarningCloud-synced folders



Putting Git repositories inside Dropbox, OneDrive, iCloud Drive, or Google Drive causes real trouble: the sync client and Git both try to manage the same files and can corrupt the repository’s internal state. Git is already your backup, and GitHub is already your cloud copy. Use a plain local folder.

title: RStudio projects and cloning a repository
section: Situation A: the repository already exists on GitHub
text:
Situation A: the repository already exists on GitHub
This is the common case: someone has given you a URL, or you accepted an assignment and GitHub created a repository for you. You want a local copy, which is called cloning.
Copy the repository URL first. On the repository’s GitHub page, click the green Code button and copy the HTTPS URL. It looks like https://github.com/owner/repository-name.git. The URL in your browser’s address bar works too.
Then use either route below.

Route 1: the RStudio menu

File > New Project > Version Control > Git
Paste the URL into Repository URL. The project directory name fills in by itself; leave it.
Set Create project as subdirectory of to your projects folder (~/gph2182, or wherever you chose above).
Click Create Project.

RStudio downloads the repository and opens it as a project.


Route 2: one line in the Console
Faster once you are comfortable, and it needs no clicking:
dir.create("~/gph2182", showWarnings = FALSE)
usethis::create_from_github("owner/repository-name", destdir = "~/gph2182")
owner/repository-name is the last two segments of the repository URL. The first line creates the parent folder if it does not exist yet, which matters because create_from_github() fails with an error if the destination folder is missing. Cloud services can also quietly remove empty folders, so leaving it in does no harm.
This requires the GitHub setup from guide 2 to be finished, because it authenticates as you.






TipIn this course



Accepting an assignment on Classroom 50 creates a private repository named like gph-gu-2182-fall-2026-weekly-exercise-01-yourusername inside the gph-2182 organization. So the one-liner is:
dir.create("~/gph2182", showWarnings = FALSE)
usethis::create_from_github(
  "gph-2182/gph-gu-2182-fall-2026-weekly-exercise-01-yourusername",
  destdir = "~/gph2182"
)
with your own username on the end.

section: Situation B: you are starting something new
text:
Situation B: you are starting something new
You have an idea, or an analysis, and nothing exists yet. Build it locally, then publish it:
usethis::create_project("~/gph2182/my-analysis")   # new project, opens in RStudio
usethis::use_git()                                 # make it a Git repository
usethis::use_github()                              # create it on GitHub and push
use_git() will offer to commit the existing files and to restart RStudio: say yes to both. use_github() creates the remote repository under your account and pushes your first commit, so the project exists on github.com when it finishes.
The menu equivalent of the first line is File > New Project > New Directory > New Project.

Write paths relative to the project root: "data/raw.csv", not "/Users/you/Desktop/data/raw.csv". The second one only works on your computer.

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
text:
You need three separate pieces of software. They are easy to confuse, so it is worth being clear about what each one is:
Install them in that order: R first, then RStudio, then Git.

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
text:
1. Install R
Download it from cloud.r-project.org and run the installer with all the default options.

macOS: choose the .pkg that matches your chip. Apple Silicon (M1 through M4) needs the arm64 build; older Intel Macs need the x86_64 build. If you pick the wrong one, R will still install but some packages will fail to load later.
Windows: click “install R for the first time”, then download the .exe.

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
text:
2. Install RStudio
Download RStudio Desktop (the free open-source edition) from posit.co and install it with the defaults.
Open RStudio once. It should find R by itself and print a banner in the Console starting with R version, followed by whatever version you just installed. If RStudio opens but the Console is empty or complains that it cannot find R, R did not install correctly: reinstall it and then restart RStudio.
Quarto, which turns your .qmd files into documents, ships inside RStudio. You do not install it separately.

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
text:
3. Install Git

macOSWindowsLinux


Open the Terminal tab in RStudio (bottom-left pane, next to Console) and run:
xcode-select --install
A system dialog appears. Click Install and wait a few minutes. This installs Apple’s command line developer tools, which include Git.
If it says command line tools are already installed, you already have Git and you are done with this step.


Download Git for Windows from git-scm.com/download/win and run the installer.
Accept every default. The defaults matter more than they look: they put git on your system path, which is what lets RStudio find it. Do not change the editor or path options unless you know why you are changing them.
After it finishes, restart RStudio. RStudio only looks for Git when it starts, so a running RStudio will not notice the new installation.


sudo apt install git      # Debian, Ubuntu
sudo dnf install git      # Fedora

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
text:
4. Check that it worked
In RStudio, click the Terminal tab (bottom-left pane, beside Console) and type:
git --version
You want a version number back, such as git version 2.39.5. Any version is fine; Git is stable and old versions work. If you get command not found, see Git is not installed or RStudio cannot find it.
Then confirm RStudio itself knows where Git lives: Tools > Global Options > Git/SVN. The “Git executable” box should hold a real path (/usr/bin/git on macOS, something like C:/Program Files/Git/bin/git.exe on Windows) and Enable version control interface for RStudio projects should be checked.

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
section: 5. Install the R packages you will need
text:
5. Install the R packages you will need
Paste this into the Console (the pane where R runs, not the Terminal) and press Enter:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "usethis", "gitcreds"))
This takes several minutes the first time. Some output scrolls by in red; that is normal progress reporting, not an error. What matters is whether the final lines say the packages were unpacked and the prompt > comes back.
If you are asked “Do you want to install from sources the package which needs compilation?”, answer no unless you have a reason to compile.






TipIn this course



Add the course textbook package as well:
install.packages("r02pro")
That gives you the gm and sahp datasets used throughout the exercises.

title: Doing a weekly exercise
text:
Once per computer: gph_setup()
gph_setup()
It installs anything missing, asks for your name and email, and walks you through creating and storing a GitHub token. Run it again any time to confirm things are still connected; it is safe to repeat.
If you would rather understand each piece, the long version is in Connecting RStudio to GitHub.

title: Doing a weekly exercise
section: Once per exercise: accept, then gph_start(N)
text:
Once per exercise: accept, then gph_start(N)

Accept the assignment. The link is on that week’s page, for example Weekly Exercise 2. This creates a private GitHub repository that belongs to you. Do it once per exercise.
Open it in RStudio. In the Console:
gph_start(2)
Use the exercise number you are working on. That is the whole step: no URL to copy, no dialog to fill in, no folder to choose. It works out which repository is yours, downloads it into ~/gph2182, and opens it as a project.

If you have not accepted yet, gph_start() says so and prints the link you need.






NoteWhere does it put things?



Wherever you already keep your course work. gph_start() looks at where your other course projects live and puts the new one beside them, so if your folder is called ~/NYU/stats or ~/grad/fall2026, that is where it goes. If you have none yet, it asks once and remembers the answer.
It also never makes a second copy: if you already have that exercise, it opens the copy you have and tells you where it is.
To keep them somewhere else, pass the folder once and it is remembered:
gph_start(3, where = "path/to/your/folder")
And the safety net: if you already have an exercise open, you do not need gph_start() at all. gph_check() and gph_submit() work from inside any copy of the repository, wherever it lives.

title: Doing a weekly exercise
section: Once for the whole semester: your in-class repository
text:
Once for the whole semester: your in-class repository
In-class exercises are different from the weekly exercises. They all live in one repository that you set up once and reuse every week.

Accept the in-class assignment on Classroom 50. Once, for the semester.
In the Console:
source("https://gph-2182.github.io/gph2182.R")   # unless already loaded
gph_inclass()

Each week, from inside that project, fetch the worksheet with the week’s number:
source("get_worksheet.R"); get_worksheet(3)
Then add both partners’ names, do the work, and commit and push before the end of class.






WarningDo not create this repository yourself



It has to be the one Classroom 50 makes, because that is the copy owned by the class and visible to the instructor. A repository you create under your own GitHub account is invisible to us, and if it is public your classmates can read your answers. If you have already made one by hand, run gph_inclass() to get the proper one and copy your worksheet files across.

title: Doing a weekly exercise
text:
Then repeat: edit, check, submit

Edit
Open exercise.qmd. Put your name in the author: field. Answer each question by replacing NULL with your code.
Keep the object names exactly as given (q1, q2, and so on). The checks look for those names, so renaming them loses points even when your code is right.


Check
gph_check()
This runs the same checks GitHub will run, on your machine, in about two seconds. You get a PASS or FAIL line per question. Fix the FAIL lines and run it again. Nothing is submitted and nobody sees the result.






gph_check() runs in a separate, clean R session on purpose. That means it cannot be fooled by an answer that only exists in your Environment pane rather than in the file, which is the most common reason work passes locally and fails on GitHub.





Submit
gph_submit()
One command does all of it: stages your files, commits them, pushes to GitHub, then waits for GitHub’s own check and tells you the result in the Console. You do not have to visit the Actions tab; the link it prints is clickable if you want to look.
It pauses for up to a couple of minutes at the end, and that is normal. Your work is already submitted by then; the wait is only for GitHub to report back. You can stop waiting at any time without affecting your submission.

When something goes wrong
gph_doctor()
It prints a ✓ or ✗ for every single thing that has to be true, in order: packages, your Git name and email, your token, whether this folder is really a repository, whether anything is uncommitted, whether anything is unpushed, and what GitHub said about your last submission. The first ✗ is your problem, and each line tells you which command fixes it.
If you are still stuck, look the exact error message up on the error messages page, then send me or Sabrina the output of gph_doctor(). That output contains no secrets and usually makes the answer obvious in one reply.

title: Error messages, decoded
section: The course commands are not loaded
text:
The course commands are not loaded
You see:
> gph_inclass()
Error in gph_inclass() : could not find function "gph_inclass"
What it means: the course helper commands are not loaded in this R session. They are not part of R, so every new session starts without them. Restarting R, opening a different project, or reopening RStudio all give you a fresh session.
Fix: run this, then try your command again.
source("https://gph-2182.github.io/gph2182.R")
You will know it worked when gph_start, gph_check and the others appear under Functions in the Environment pane.
Permanent fix: run gph_setup() and say yes when it offers to load the commands automatically. It saves a copy in your home folder and loads it at every startup, so you never type the source() line again.

title: Error messages, decoded
section: Git is not installed, or RStudio cannot find it
text:
Git is not installed, or RStudio cannot find it
You see: git: command not found, or bash: git: No such file or directory, or RStudio’s Tools > Global Options > Git/SVN box is empty.
What it means: Git is a separate program from R and RStudio, and either it was never installed or RStudio has not noticed it.
Fix:

macOS: run xcode-select --install in the RStudio Terminal tab.
Windows: install Git for Windows from git-scm.com/download/win, accepting all defaults.
Then restart RStudio. It only looks for Git at startup, so a running RStudio will not see a fresh installation.

If Git is installed but the Git/SVN box is still empty, type the path in yourself: /usr/bin/git on macOS, C:/Program Files/Git/bin/git.exe on Windows. Then restart RStudio.
Full instructions: Installing R, RStudio, and Git.

title: Error messages, decoded
section: There is no Git tab in RStudio
text:
There is no Git tab in RStudio
You see: the top-right pane shows Environment, History, and Connections, but no Git.
What it means: almost always that you opened a plain folder or a loose file rather than an RStudio project that is also a Git repository.
Fix, in order of likelihood:

Check the top-right corner of the window. If it says “Project: (None)”, you do not have a project open. Open the .Rproj file in the folder, or use File > Recent Projects.
If you downloaded the repository as a ZIP from GitHub, that copy is not a repository at all: the Git history is not included in a ZIP. Delete it and clone properly, per guide 3.
If the project is open and it really was cloned, check Tools > Global Options > Git/SVN and confirm Enable version control interface is ticked and the Git path is filled in. Restart RStudio afterward.

title: Error messages, decoded
section: Git does not know your name
text:
Git does not know your name
You see:
*** Please tell me who you are.
Run
  git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
  git config --global user.name "Your Name"
What it means: Git stamps every commit with an author and refuses to commit without one.
Fix: in the RStudio Console:
usethis::use_git_config(
  user.name  = "Your Name",
  user.email = "you@example.edu"
)
Use the email on your GitHub account, so your commits are credited to your profile. Then commit again.

title: Error messages, decoded
text:
Your password is rejected
You see: Authentication failed, Invalid username or password, fatal: Authentication failed for 'https://github.com/...', or remote: Support for password authentication was removed on August 13, 2021.
What it means: GitHub does not accept account passwords for Git operations. It needs a personal access token. If RStudio is prompting you for a password at all, no token is stored.
Fix:
usethis::create_github_token()   # opens GitHub; set Expiration to a date you choose
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()         # paste the token here
usethis::git_sitrep()            # confirm it is stored
If this used to work and just stopped, your old token expired. The fix is the same: generate a new one and store it with gitcreds_set(), choosing replace when it offers the menu.
Full walkthrough: Connecting RStudio to GitHub.

title: Error messages, decoded
text:
Repository not found
You see: remote: Repository not found, or fatal: repository 'https://github.com/...' not found.
What it means: GitHub is saying “either that repository does not exist, or you are not allowed to see it”. It gives the same message for both, on purpose, so that private repository names cannot be probed.
Check, in order:

Typo in the URL. Owner and repository name are both case-sensitive in practice. Copy the URL from your browser rather than retyping it.
You are not signed in as the right account. Run usethis::git_sitrep() and look at the GitHub user it reports. A stored token for a personal account cannot see a private organization repository.
You do not have access yet. If it is private and belongs to someone else, you need to be added as a collaborator or organization member.







TipIn this course



This usually means you have not accepted the GitHub organization invitation that was emailed to you, or it expired after seven days. Ask for a fresh invitation, accept it, then try again.

title: Error messages, decoded
text:
Updates were rejected
You see:
! [rejected]  main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
      not have locally.
What it means: GitHub has commits that your computer does not. Git refuses to push, because doing so would erase them. This is Git protecting you.
Fix: click Pull, then Push. That downloads the missing commits and merges them with yours.
This happens most often when you edited a file directly on github.com in the browser, or worked from a second computer. If the pull produces a conflict, see merge conflict below.

title: Error messages, decoded
text:
Pull blocked by local changes
You see: error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge followed by a file name.
What it means: you have uncommitted edits to a file that the incoming commits also change. Git will not silently discard your edits.
Fix: commit your edits first, then pull.
git add .
git commit -m "Work in progress"
git pull
Committing is the right move even if the work is unfinished. A commit is a private checkpoint, not a publication, and you can always tidy the history later.

title: Error messages, decoded
text:
Merge conflict
You see: markers like these inside one of your files, and Git reports CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in exercise.qmd.
<<<<<<< HEAD
mean_age <- mean(df$age, na.rm = TRUE)
=======
mean_age <- mean(df$age)
>>>>>>> origin/main
What it means: two commits changed the same lines and Git will not guess which one wins. The text between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is yours; the text between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming version.
Fix: open the file, decide what the lines should say (possibly a blend of both), delete all three marker lines, save, then stage and commit. That commit is the resolution.
Nothing is broken while a conflict is open, and nothing is lost. Take your time.

title: Error messages, decoded
text:
Not a git repository
You see: fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git.
What it means: you are running a Git command in a folder that Git does not manage.
Fix: you are probably in the wrong directory. Check with getwd() in the Console, and open the right project. If this folder genuinely should be a repository, make it one with usethis::use_git().

title: Error messages, decoded
text:
Permission denied (publickey)
You see: git@github.com: Permission denied (publickey). fatal: Could not read from remote repository.
What it means: the repository’s remote URL uses SSH (git@github.com:...), but GitHub does not have an SSH key that matches yours.
Fix, the simple way: switch that repository to HTTPS, which uses the token you already have.
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/owner/repository-name.git
Fix, the other way: set up an SSH key, as described in the Happy Git with R SSH chapter.

title: Error messages, decoded
section: create_from_github() says the folder does not exist
text:
create_from_github() says the folder does not exist
You see: an error from usethis::create_from_github() complaining that the destdir path does not exist or is not a directory.
What it means: create_from_github() will not create the parent folder for you; it requires it to be there already.
Fix: create it first, in the same block:
dir.create("~/gph2182", showWarnings = FALSE)
usethis::create_from_github("owner/repository-name", destdir = "~/gph2182")
showWarnings = FALSE makes the first line harmless when the folder already exists.

title: Error messages, decoded
text:
File too large
You see: remote: error: File data/big.csv is 214.00 MB; this exceeds GitHub's file size limit of 100.00 MB.
What it means: GitHub refuses individual files over 100 MB, and warns above 50 MB. The whole push fails, not just that file.
Fix: stop tracking the file, and ignore it going forward.
git rm --cached data/big.csv
usethis::use_git_ignore("data/big.csv")
Then commit and push again. Note that if the large file is already in an earlier commit, removing it now is not enough: the history still contains it, and cleaning that up is a bigger job. It is far easier to keep large data out of Git from the start, and to store it elsewhere with a script that downloads it.

title: Error messages, decoded
section: You are in detached HEAD state
text:
You are in detached HEAD state
You see: You are in 'detached HEAD' state, usually after clicking around in the History view.
What it means: you are looking at an old commit rather than at the tip of a branch. It is a viewing mode, not damage. Commits made here can be hard to find later.
Fix: go back to your branch.
git checkout main
If you made commits while detached and want to keep them, git switch -c rescue-branch before checking out main, and ask for help merging them.

title: Error messages, decoded
section: Push succeeds but GitHub looks unchanged
text:
Push succeeds but GitHub looks unchanged
You see: Everything up-to-date, or a successful push, but the repository page on github.com does not show your work.
Check three things:

Which branch you are on. The Git tab shows it at the top right of the pane. If you are on a branch other than main, your commits went there; GitHub’s repository page shows main by default. Use the branch dropdown on GitHub to look, then merge or open a pull request.
Which repository you are looking at. Confusing a fork, a template, and your own copy is easy. Run git remote -v and compare it against the URL in your browser.
Whether you actually committed. Everything up-to-date means there were no new commits to send. Saved but uncommitted files are still only on your disk. Check the Git tab: any files still listed are not committed.

title: Error messages, decoded
text:
Still stuck?
Before asking anyone, collect these three things. With them, almost any question gets answered in one reply; without them, the answer is always “what does the error say?”.

The exact error text, copied as text or a screenshot. Not a paraphrase: the specific words are what identify the problem.
The output of usethis::git_sitrep(), which shows your Git identity, your token, and the repository’s remote in one block. It contains no secrets, so it is safe to share.
What you did immediately before, in one sentence.

Pasting all three into an AI assistant resolves most setup problems in a couple of turns. If it does not, bring the same three things to office hours or an email.

title: Connecting RStudio to GitHub
text:
This is the step that fails most often, and always for one of two reasons: Git does not know who you are, or GitHub will not accept your password. Both are fixed below, permanently, in about ten minutes.
Work through the five steps in order. Everything goes in the RStudio Console (the pane where R runs), not the Terminal.

title: Connecting RStudio to GitHub
text:
1. Create a GitHub account
Sign up at github.com/signup. Two pieces of advice you will be glad of later:

Choose a username you would put on a CV. It becomes part of every URL you share, it is public, and changing it later breaks your links. Something close to your real name works well.
Use an email address you will keep. If you sign up with a school address, add a personal one as a secondary email under Settings > Emails before you graduate, so you do not lose the account when the school address is closed.







TipIn this course



Sign up with your NYU address so the roster can match your account to your NetID. You will also be invited to the course GitHub organization by email: accept that invitation before anything else, because the assignment links do not work until you are a member. Invitations expire after seven days.

title: Connecting RStudio to GitHub
text:
2. Tell Git who you are
Git stamps every commit with a name and an email. It refuses to commit until you supply them.
install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))   # if you have not already

usethis::use_git_config(
  user.name  = "Your Name",
  user.email = "you@example.edu"
)
Use the email address attached to your GitHub account. If the two do not match, your commits will still work but GitHub will not credit them to your profile.
The name is a display name, not a login, so write it the way you would sign an email. A username with no spaces works too.

title: Connecting RStudio to GitHub
text:
3. Create a personal access token
GitHub stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations in 2021. When RStudio asks you to push and you type your GitHub password, it will be rejected every time. You need a personal access token (PAT) instead: a long random string that acts as a password for Git alone, and that you can revoke without touching your account.
usethis::create_github_token()
This opens GitHub in your browser with the right permissions already ticked. On that page:

Replace the placeholder Note (DESCRIBE THE TOKEN'S USE CASE) with something you will recognize later, such as RStudio on my laptop.
Set the Expiration. The default is 30 days, which is almost never what you want: your pushes will silently start failing a month from now. Open the dropdown, choose Custom, and pick a date at the end of your project or term.
Leave the checked scopes alone. usethis has already selected repo, user, gist, and workflow, which is what RStudio needs.
Scroll down and click Generate token.







ImportantCopy the token now



The token is shown exactly once. Copy it before you leave the page. If you lose it, nothing is broken, you just generate a new one and start this step again.
Treat it like a password: never paste it into a script, a .qmd file, or a chat message, and never commit it. If it ever leaks, delete it under Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens and make a new one.








TipIn this course



Set the expiration to December 31, 2026, which covers the whole semester with room to spare. A 30-day default token expires in the middle of October, which is exactly when you do not want to be debugging authentication.

title: Connecting RStudio to GitHub
text:
4. Store the token
Back in the RStudio Console:
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
Paste the token when prompted and press Enter. It goes into your operating system’s credential store (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows), so you do this once per computer, not once per project.
If a token is already stored, gitcreds_set() shows you a short menu; choose the option to replace it.

title: Connecting RStudio to GitHub
text:
5. Check the whole setup
usethis::git_sitrep()
This prints a situation report. These are the lines that matter:
Git config (global)
* Name: 'Your Name'
* Email: 'you@example.edu'
...
GitHub
* Default GitHub host: 'https://github.com'
* Personal access token for 'https://github.com': '<discovered>'
* GitHub user: 'yourusername'
* Token scopes: 'gist, repo, user, workflow'
Name and email filled in, a token discovered, and a GitHub username shown means you are connected. If the token line says <unset>, step 4 did not take effect: run gitcreds::gitcreds_set() again.
Do not worry about the other lines. Vaccinated: FALSE and an unset global gitignore are suggestions, not problems, and nothing on this page depends on them.

title: Connecting RStudio to GitHub
text:
When your token expires
Tokens are supposed to expire. When yours does, pushes start failing with an authentication error even though nothing about your setup changed. GitHub emails you a warning a week beforehand.
The fix is steps 3 and 4 again:
usethis::create_github_token()   # generate a fresh one
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()         # choose "replace" and paste it
You do not need to touch your repositories, and no work is lost.

title: Connecting RStudio to GitHub
text:
A note on SSH keys
There is a second way to authenticate, using an SSH key pair instead of a token. It is a little more setup once and a little less maintenance afterward, and it is a perfectly good choice if you already have keys.
Tokens are recommended here because they work identically on every operating system, they are what usethis automates, and expiry makes them safer on a shared or borrowed machine. If you want SSH, usethis::use_git_protocol("ssh") and the Happy Git with R chapter cover it.

title: Connecting RStudio to GitHub
text:

You are connected. Now set up an RStudio project so you have somewhere to put the work.

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
text:
Saving a file and saving your work are different things. Git puts three checkpoints between the file on your disk and the copy on GitHub, and almost every confusion about Git comes from collapsing them.








Step
What it does
Where the work now is




Save (Ctrl/Cmd+S)
Writes your edits to the file
On your disk only


Stage (tick the box)
Marks a file as part of the next snapshot
Chosen, not yet recorded


Commit
Records a permanent snapshot with a message
In your local history


Push
Uploads your commits to GitHub
On GitHub, visible to others



The consequence worth memorizing: a commit is not on GitHub until you push. Every term, someone commits diligently all week, never pushes, and believes the work was submitted. Only what is pushed exists to anyone but you.
Pull is the reverse of push: it brings down commits made elsewhere (by a collaborator, by your other laptop, or by an edit you made on github.com in the browser).

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
text:
The routine
Once your project is open in RStudio, you will use the Git tab in the top-right pane. Files appear there as soon as they change.

1. Pull before you start
Click the blue Pull arrow. If you are the only person working, this usually reports “Already up to date”, which takes a second and saves you the rejected push described below.


2. Do your work, and save
Nothing Git-related here. Edit, save, run, render.


3. Stage what belongs in this snapshot
In the Git tab, tick the Staged checkbox next to each file you want to include. The two-letter status codes mean:







Code
Meaning




M
Modified: the file existed and you changed it


A
Added: a new file, now staged


?
Untracked: a new file Git has never seen (git status calls it ??)


D
Deleted


R
Renamed



Stage your source files. Do not stage things that are generated, huge, or private: see what not to commit.


4. Commit
Click Commit. A window opens showing your staged changes line by line, with additions in green and deletions in red. Read that diff: it is the cheapest bug check you will ever get.
Write a message in the box and click Commit.
A good message says what changed and why, in the present tense, in one line:

Good: Add Q3 boxplot and fix filter on year
Good: Correct sample size in the summary table
Less useful: update, stuff, asdf, final FINAL v2

You are writing to your future self, who will scroll this history in three months looking for the commit where something broke.


5. Push
Close the commit window and click the green Push arrow. When it finishes, your work is on GitHub.
If Push asks for a username and password, your token is not set up: go back to guide 2. If it reports that updates were rejected, click Pull first, then Push again.


6. Confirm
Open the repository on github.com and look at it. Your files should be there, with your commit message and a timestamp beside them. This takes five seconds and is the only real proof that the work is submitted.






TipIn this course



After you push, click the Actions tab on your repository page. Within about two minutes the autograder reports which questions passed. You can revise and push as often as you like before the deadline: only the final state counts, so a red X on an early attempt costs you nothing.

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
text:
What not to commit
Git is for source, not for output or secrets.







Do commit
Do not commit




.R and .qmd files
Tokens, passwords, API keys


Small input data
Data you are not allowed to redistribute


.gitignore, README.md, .Rproj
Files over 100 MB (GitHub refuses them)


Anything needed to reproduce the work
.Rproj.user/, .Rhistory, .RData



A .gitignore file lists patterns Git should ignore, so those files stop appearing in the Git tab entirely. RStudio creates a sensible one for you when it makes a project. To add to it:
usethis::use_git_ignore(c("*.csv", "secrets.R"))






Important



Committing a secret and then deleting it does not remove it: it stays in the history and is still readable. If you push a token or password, revoke it immediately on GitHub and issue a new one. That is the fix; editing the file is not.

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
section: The same thing in the Terminal
text:
The same thing in the Terminal
The Git tab is a friendly front end for a handful of commands. If you prefer typing, or you are on a machine without RStudio, these are the equivalents. Run them in the RStudio Terminal tab or any shell, from inside the project folder.
git status                        # what has changed, and what is staged
git add exercise.qmd              # stage one file
git add .                         # stage everything changed
git commit -m "Add Q3 boxplot"    # record a snapshot
git push                          # upload to GitHub
git pull                          # download from GitHub
git log --oneline                 # your history, one commit per line
git status is the single most useful command in Git. When you are lost, run it: it tells you where you are and usually suggests the command you want next.

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
text:
Undoing things
Nothing here loses committed work. Git makes it genuinely hard to destroy something you have committed, which is most of the point of using it.








You want to
In RStudio
In the Terminal




Unstage a file
Untick its Staged box
git restore --staged FILE


Throw away uncommitted edits to a file
Git tab > select > More > Revert
git restore FILE


Fix the message on the last commit
Commit window > tick Amend previous commit
git commit --amend


See what changed in a file
Git tab > select > Diff
git diff FILE


Look at an old version
Git tab > History (clock icon)
git log -p FILE









Warning



Reverting uncommitted changes is the one genuinely destructive action in that table. Those edits were never recorded, so Git cannot bring them back. Commit first when you are unsure: a messy commit is always better than lost work.


Only amend a commit you have not pushed yet. Amending rewrites history, and rewriting history that others have already pulled creates a mess for them.

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
section: When two people edit the same lines
text:
When two people edit the same lines
If you and a collaborator change the same lines of the same file, a pull produces a merge conflict. Git marks the disagreement inside the file:
<<<<<<< HEAD
mean_age <- mean(df$age, na.rm = TRUE)
=======
mean_age <- mean(df$age)
>>>>>>> origin/main
To resolve it: open the file, delete the three marker lines, keep the code you want (which may be a blend of both), save, then stage and commit as usual. The commit that follows is the resolution.
Conflicts are normal collaboration, not a failure. They are also much rarer when everyone pulls before starting and pushes when they finish.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course Description
R is one of the most popular programming languages in statistics and data science. This course will introduce various R programming topics, including R objects, data visualization, data import & export, data manipulation, creating functions and iterations for statistical simulations, and writing high-quality reports with R Markdown. The course will focus on public health datasets as illustrations to best meet the practical needs of GPH students but is also open to those of other backgrounds. By the end of the course, students will be able to comfortably program in R for effective data preprocessing, analysis and presentation. This course does not require prior experience in programming or statistics and serves as a foundation for other courses in biostatistics, epidemiology, and data science.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course Overview
This course equips graduate students with foundational and modern computing skills for reproducible public health data science. Using a dual-track pedagogical approach, students learn fundamental computational primitives alongside modern, expressive tidyverse workflows. The curriculum covers Quarto reproducible publishing, vectors, matrices, lists, data frames, publication-quality graphics with ggplot2, robust data wrangling with dplyr and tidyr, string and factor manipulation, functional programming with purrr, and Monte Carlo simulation. Students will also master responsible, ethical AI-assisted programming to accelerate learning, debugging, and code documentation while building genuine human fluency.

You type commands into the Console; R evaluates them and prints results.

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:
Objects and Variable Assignment
We store values in named objects using the assignment operator <- (Alt + - or Option + -):
# Assigning a value
participant_age <- 28
height_m <- 1.75
weight_kg <- 68.5

# Using objects in expressions
bmi <- weight_kg / (height_m^2)
bmi

Names must start with a letter and can contain letters, numbers, _, and ..
R is case-sensitive (bmi \(\neq\) BMI).

title: Week 1: Welcome & The Modern R Toolkit
text:

Functions take arguments (inputs) and return an output:
# Rounding
round(bmi, digits = 1)

# Summary statistics
vals <- c(10, 20, 30, NA)
mean(vals, na.rm = TRUE)
Getting help in R:

?round or help(round) — opens the official documentation.
example(round) — runs examples from the help page.

mean_age
